message.content:
The answer depends on what one means by a finite expectation.
In the usual measure theoretic sense, a finite expectation means the variable is integrable.
If X and Y are both integrable, then X plus Y is integrable.
In that sense, no such example exists.
The triangle inequality gives the absolute bound needed for the sum.
The linearity of expectation then applies safely.
However, some elementary treatments use conditional convergence of a series to define expectation.
Under that weaker convention, a discrete variable can have a finite mean without an absolutely summable tail.
Then cancellations between positive and negative values can make the series converge.
Another variable can disturb those cancellations enough to break convergence for the sum.
This makes an example possible.
Begin with a discrete integer valued variable Z.
Give Z probabilities at large positive integers and large negative integers.
Make the positive and negative probabilities symmetric.
Make the probabilities decay slowly enough that the absolute sum diverges.
Then the ordinary series for the mean may converge to zero.
Define X to be Z.
Define Y to be negative Z plus a small discrete correction.
Choose the correction so that Y still has a conditionally finite mean.
Choose it so that X plus Y has a tail with divergent one sided sums.
Then the series for the expectation of X plus Y may fail to converge.
The separate means can remain finite in the conditional sense.
Thus, yes, under a conditional convention such variables exist, but under an integrability convention they do not, because the expectation of the sum may fail when tails are not controlled, the exact issue beneath remains.
